frameworks.name: New York State Social Emotional Learning Benchmarks (Equity Revisions)
frameworks.notes: Original benchmarks 2018; equity revisions 2022. Three goals: (1) self-awareness that nurtures identity and agency, (2) social awareness and interpersonal skills for supportive relationships, (3) intentional decision-making. Items here are the 10 base indicators (1A-3C); each has grade-band indicators (K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-10, 11-12) in the source. Titles are short paraphrases. Text was read from the Children's Institute-hosted copy of NYSED's document (nysed.gov's own PDF refused the download); confirm against NYSED's PDF before verifying. CASEL tags follow the document's own footnote (goal 1 = self-awareness and self-management, goal 2 = social awareness and relationship skills, goal 3 = responsible decision-making); the split within goals is a judgment call for the reviewer.

items.title: Understand emotions and how they relate to actions
items.summary: Identify one's emotions, see how they connect to what one does, and use that understanding to guide actions.

items.title: Explore personal and group identity
items.summary: Reflect on personal and group identity, including cultural background, and find outside supports for identity development.

items.title: Set and work toward goals; learn from mistakes
items.summary: Set personal and academic goals, take risks, own mistakes, and use them to grow.

items.title: Build empathy for others' feelings and perspectives
items.summary: Recognize and understand that other people feel and react differently based on their experiences and cultures.

items.title: Affirm identities, similarities and differences
items.summary: Recognize and affirm individual and group identities and differences, and engage respectfully in difficult conversations.

items.title: Communicate and interact across lines of difference
items.summary: Use a range of communication and social skills with individuals and groups, with empathy in every interaction.

items.title: Prevent, manage and resolve conflicts
items.summary: Prevent, manage or resolve conflicts, including those involving injustice, and express agreement or disagreement respectfully.

items.title: Consider safety, well-being and context in decisions
items.summary: Weigh individual and collective social, emotional and physical safety and the social context when making decisions.

items.title: Apply decision-making skills to shape outcomes
items.summary: Use decision-making skills to influence outcomes and strengthen agency in social and academic life.

items.title: Act to support school and community well-being
items.summary: Take action for the well-being of school and community, including standing against bias and injustice.

frameworks.name: New York State Portrait of a Graduate
frameworks.issuingBody: New York State Board of Regents / NYSED
frameworks.notes: Six interconnected attributes grounded in Culturally Responsive-Sustaining Education. Read from NYSED's one-page Portrait PDF (nysed.gov/sites/default/files/programs/grad-measures/portrait-of-a-graduate.pdf). Summaries are paraphrases.

items.title: Academically Prepared
items.summary: Strong foundation in the NYS learning standards, ready for college, careers, civic engagement, service and life.

items.title: Creative Innovator
items.summary: Uses imagination, curiosity and flexible thinking to solve problems and develop new ideas while adapting to change.

items.title: Critical Thinker
items.summary: Analyzes information, weighs evidence and finds connections across subjects to address complex issues.

items.title: Effective Communicator
items.summary: Expresses ideas clearly through speaking, writing and media, and listens to different perspectives.

items.title: Global Citizen
items.summary: Acts responsibly and ethically in local, global and digital communities and contributes to a diverse, democratic society.

items.title: Reflective and Future Focused
items.summary: Reflects on strengths and growth areas, sets goals, keeps supportive relationships and makes responsible decisions that protect well-being.

Picks like helping a tired friend clean up or lifting a box together are small acts for the good of the team. Limit: the team is two or three children, not a school or community.

alignments.framework: New York State Social Emotional Learning Benchmarks (Equity Revisions)
alignments.rationale: Tune Your Brain game "Wait for It" (tagged self-management). FNE's catalog description: "Listen to a waiting problem, then pick what helps you wait." Each round puts a child in a moment of wanting something now or feeling mad (dinner in ten minutes, a turn on the slide, losing a game) and the child picks what helps them wait, such as a deep breath or counting to ten. That links a feeling or urge to a calming action. Limit: the main skill is impulse control, and most rounds name a want rather than an emotion, so it is a partial match.

alignments.framework: New York State Social Emotional Learning Benchmarks (Equity Revisions)
alignments.rationale: Tune Your Brain game "Wait for It" (tagged self-management). FNE's catalog description: "Listen to a waiting problem, then pick what helps you wait." Choosing to wait and say okay instead of grabbing or shouting is a small decision that shapes how the moment goes. Limit: one-step choices; no weighing of options.

alignments.framework: New York State Social Emotional Learning Benchmarks (Equity Revisions)
alignments.rationale: Tune Your Brain game "Stop and Think" (tagged responsible decision-making). FNE's catalog description: "Listen to a problem, stop and think, then pick the safe choice." Rounds present a safety moment (a ball rolling into the street, a stranger offering candy, a pill on the floor, a hot stove, a friend climbing a high fence) and the child pauses and picks the safe choice, usually involving a grown-up. That is weighing safety when making a decision, which the benchmark names. Limit: simple K-2 safety rules; it does not weigh social context.

alignments.framework: New York State Social Emotional Learning Benchmarks (Equity Revisions)
alignments.rationale: Tune Your Brain game "Stop and Think" (tagged responsible decision-making). FNE's catalog description: "Listen to a problem, stop and think, then pick the safe choice." The child stops, thinks and then chooses, so it practises the pause before a decision. Limit: one right answer per round; no weighing of several options and no reflection afterward.

alignments.framework: New York State Social Emotional Learning Benchmarks (Equity Revisions)
alignments.rationale: Tune Your Brain game "My Feelings Today" (tagged self-awareness). FNE's catalog description: "Say how you feel, where you feel it and what helps. Only you see it." A private check-in. The child picks how they feel (up to two feelings), where they feel it in their body and what helps, then sees a card built from their own picks. That is naming one's own emotion and connecting it to what helps, which is the skill the benchmark describes. Nothing is saved or scored.

alignments.framework: New York State Portrait of a Graduate
alignments.rationale: Tune Your Brain game "My Feelings Today" (tagged self-awareness). FNE's catalog description: "Say how you feel, where you feel it and what helps. Only you see it." The check-in asks the child to stop and think about their own feelings and what helps them. Limit: about a minute long; it does not ask about strengths, goals or growth.

alignments.framework: New York State Social Emotional Learning Benchmarks (Equity Revisions)
alignments.rationale: Tune Your Brain game "Team Pick" (tagged self-management and relationship skills). FNE's catalog description: "Work through being picked last for a team: what you feel, what could happen and what to do." The player works through being picked last for a team in five steps (see what is happening, what it feels like, what could happen, what to do, a private reflection on what helps them calm down). That ties a feeling to a choice of action, which is what the benchmark describes.

alignments.framework: New York State Social Emotional Learning Benchmarks (Equity Revisions)
alignments.rationale: Tune Your Brain game "Team Pick" (tagged self-management and relationship skills). FNE's catalog description: "Work through being picked last for a team: what you feel, what could happen and what to do." The best moves include telling friends calmly how it felt, without blame. Limit: one step in a five-step story.

alignments.framework: New York State Social Emotional Learning Benchmarks (Equity Revisions)
alignments.rationale: Tune Your Brain game "Team Pick" (tagged self-management and relationship skills). FNE's catalog description: "Work through being picked last for a team: what you feel, what could happen and what to do." Talking to the friends who picked is a way to handle a hurt before it becomes a conflict. Limit: the story is about a hurt feeling, not a two-sided disagreement.

alignments.framework: New York State Portrait of a Graduate
alignments.rationale: Tune Your Brain game "Team Pick" (tagged self-management and relationship skills). FNE's catalog description: "Work through being picked last for a team: what you feel, what could happen and what to do." The closing private reflection asks what helps the player settle, and the story ends in a choice that protects both their feelings and their friendships. Limit: one reflection question; it does not ask about strengths or goals.

alignments.framework: New York State Social Emotional Learning Benchmarks (Equity Revisions)
alignments.rationale: Tune Your Brain game "Strength Spotter" (tagged self-awareness). FNE's catalog description: "Notice what someone does, spot the strengths it shows, then think about your own." After stories about other children, the child picks strengths that sound like them and says where they have used them, which is reflecting on who they are. Limit: personal strengths only; no cultural or group identity.

alignments.framework: New York State Portrait of a Graduate
alignments.rationale: Tune Your Brain game "Strength Spotter" (tagged self-awareness). FNE's catalog description: "Notice what someone does, spot the strengths it shows, then think about your own." The child notices what a character does, picks strengths that sound like them, says where they use them and picks one small way to grow a strength. That is reflecting on strengths and growth areas. Limit: a private check-in with nothing saved or scored.

alignments.framework: New York State Social Emotional Learning Benchmarks (Equity Revisions)
alignments.rationale: Tune Your Brain game "Strength Spotter" (tagged self-awareness). FNE's catalog description: "Notice what someone does, spot the strengths it shows, then think about your own." The last step offers one small way to grow the strength they picked (for example, breaking a big job into three small steps), a small step toward a personal goal. Limit: one step, no follow-up.

alignments.framework: New York State Social Emotional Learning Benchmarks (Equity Revisions)
alignments.rationale: Tune Your Brain game "Peace Table" (tagged relationship skills and social awareness). FNE's catalog description: "Two kids disagree. Say what happened, listen, and find a fair plan together." Each story is two children who both want the same thing. The player says what happened and how they feel, listens to the other side and finds a fair plan together. That is managing and resolving a conflict respectfully.

alignments.framework: New York State Social Emotional Learning Benchmarks (Equity Revisions)
alignments.rationale: Tune Your Brain game "Peace Table" (tagged relationship skills and social awareness). FNE's catalog description: "Two kids disagree. alignments.framework: New York State Social Emotional Learning Benchmarks (Equity Revisions)

Say what happened, listen, and find a fair plan together." A step asks what the player notices about the other child's side, so they practise seeing that the other child also has a reason and a feeling. Limit: one step; empathy is not the main skill.

alignments.framework: New York State Social Emotional Learning Benchmarks (Equity Revisions)
alignments.rationale: Tune Your Brain game "Peace Table" (tagged relationship skills and social awareness). FNE's catalog description: "Two kids disagree. Say what happened, listen, and find a fair plan together." Choices include how to say what you need calmly instead of attacking ("always" statements). Limit: used to settle a disagreement, not to communicate across differences.

alignments.framework: New York State Portrait of a Graduate
alignments.rationale: Tune Your Brain game "Peace Table" (tagged relationship skills and social awareness). FNE's catalog description: "Two kids disagree. Say what happened, listen, and find a fair plan together." Saying what happened and how you feel, and listening to the other child, are the speaking and listening parts of communication. Limit: choosing among options; no free writing.

FNE's catalog description: "Work through a team-project problem: see what is happening, who it affects and what to do." The player works through a team-project problem in five steps (recognize, understand the impact, consider options, choose, reflect), with feedback on every choice. Weighing options and choosing is the decision-making cycle the benchmark describes.

alignments.framework: New York State Social Emotional Learning Benchmarks (Equity Revisions)
alignments.rationale: Tune Your Brain game "Choice Quest" (tagged social awareness, relationship skills and responsible decision-making). FNE's catalog description: "Work through a team-project problem: see what is happening, who it affects and what to do." One step asks who the problem affects, and the best answers consider why a teammate may be stuck before judging her. Limit: one step of five.

alignments.framework: New York State Social Emotional Learning Benchmarks (Equity Revisions)
alignments.rationale: Tune Your Brain game "Choice Quest" (tagged social awareness, relationship skills and responsible decision-making). FNE's catalog description: "Work through a team-project problem: see what is happening, who it affects and what to do." The careful moves involve talking with the teammate about a problem that could turn into a conflict. Limit: a missed deadline, not a direct disagreement.

alignments.framework: New York State Portrait of a Graduate
alignments.rationale: Tune Your Brain game "Choice Quest" (tagged social awareness, relationship skills and responsible decision-making). FNE's catalog description: "Work through a team-project problem: see what is happening, who it affects and what to do." The story rewards finding out what is really happening before judging a teammate. Limit: facts in a team situation, not evaluating sources.

alignments.framework: New York State Portrait of a Graduate
alignments.rationale: Tune Your Brain game "Choice Quest" (tagged social awareness, relationship skills and responsible decision-making). FNE's catalog description: "Work through a team-project problem: see what is happening, who it affects and what to do." The careful moves involve asking the teammate and saying what you noticed, and one option is telling a trusted adult, so the player practises putting a concern into words. Limit: choosing among options; no free writing.

alignments.framework: New York State Social Emotional Learning Benchmarks (Equity Revisions)
alignments.rationale: Tune Your Brain game "Fix-It Workshop" (tagged responsible decision-making). FNE's catalog description: "Find a problem at school, listen to the people it affects, and try a small fix." The player takes a real school problem (for example a slow lunch line), observes it, asks the people it affects, chooses an idea and tries a small fix. That is taking action for the well-being of the school community.

alignments.framework: New York State Portrait of a Graduate
alignments.rationale: Tune Your Brain game "Fix-It Workshop" (tagged responsible decision-making). FNE's catalog description: "Find a problem at school, listen to the people it affects, and try a small fix." The idea step offers three workable ideas, each with a strength and a cost, and the player chooses one and tries it. Finding the real problem and weighing different ideas is creative problem solving. Limit: choosing among written ideas; the player does not invent their own.

alignments.framework: New York State Social Emotional Learning Benchmarks (Equity Revisions)
alignments.rationale: Tune Your Brain game "Fix-It Workshop" (tagged responsible decision-making). FNE's catalog description: "Find a problem at school, listen to the people it affects, and try a small fix." The player asks the people the problem affects (other kids, lunch staff) what they notice. Limit: listening for facts about a problem, not understanding someone's feelings in depth.

alignments.framework: New York State Social Emotional Learning Benchmarks (Equity Revisions)
alignments.rationale: Tune Your Brain game "Fix-It Workshop" (tagged responsible decision-making). FNE's catalog description: "Find a problem at school, listen to the people it affects, and try a small fix." The five-step cycle (listen, name the real problem, pick an idea, choose how to act, reflect) is a decision-making process. Limit: the focus is designing a fix, not a personal choice.

alignments.framework: New York State Portrait of a Graduate
alignments.rationale: Tune Your Brain game "Fix-It Workshop" (tagged responsible decision-making). FNE's catalog description: "Find a problem at school, listen to the people it affects, and try a small fix." The player watches and times the problem before deciding what is wrong, so they use evidence before jumping to a fix.

alignments.rationale: Tune Your Brain game "Fix-It Workshop" (tagged responsible decision-making). FNE's catalog description: "Find a problem at school, listen to the people it affects, and try a small fix." Working to improve a shared school space is a small act as a member of a local community. Limit: school-level only.

alignments.rationale: Tune Your Brain game "Reading Detective" (a literacy-domain game). FNE's catalog description: "Read the clues in a short mystery, pick your answer, then prove it with the text." The player reads a short mystery, picks an answer and then taps the sentence in the text that proves it. Backing an answer with evidence from the text is the evidence-weighing part of critical thinking. Limit: short passages at an easy reading level; no source or bias analysis.

alignments.framework: New York State Social Emotional Learning Benchmarks (Equity Revisions)
alignments.rationale: Tune Your Brain game "Walk in My Shoes" (tagged social awareness). FNE's catalog description: "Read about someone, work out how they feel, then find the sentence that shows it." The child reads about someone (a new student alone at lunch, a child whose clay dragon broke), works out how they feel and what they need, then taps the sentence that shows it. Reading another person's feelings from what they do and say is the empathy skill the benchmark describes. Limit: reading-based scenes at grades 3 to 5.

alignments.framework: New York State Social Emotional Learning Benchmarks (Equity Revisions)
alignments.rationale: Tune Your Brain game "Many Ways to Be" (tagged social awareness). FNE's catalog description: "Read about people who are different, then pick the respectful answer and the proof." The child reads about people who are different (a different lunch, a language at home, a wheelchair at recess) and picks the respectful answer, then the sentence that shows why. That is recognizing differences and responding to them respectfully. Limit: classroom-sized situations; no harder conversations about identity.

alignments.framework: New York State Social Emotional Learning Benchmarks (Equity Revisions)
alignments.rationale: Tune Your Brain game "Many Ways to Be" (tagged social awareness). FNE's catalog description: "Read about people who are different, then pick the respectful answer and the proof." The respectful answers depend on understanding why a difference matters to the other child. Limit: the focus is on respectful responses more than on empathy for a feeling.

alignments.framework: New York State Portrait of a Graduate
alignments.rationale: Tune Your Brain game "Many Ways to Be" (tagged social awareness). FNE's catalog description: "Read about people who are different, then pick the respectful answer and the proof." Respecting different languages, foods and abilities in a shared school is part of belonging to a diverse community. Limit: classroom situations; no civic or global content.

alignments.rationale: Tune Your Brain game "What Helps Me" (tagged self-awareness). FNE's catalog description: "Pick what helps you learn and focus, then try one idea. Only you see it." A private check-in. The child picks what helps them learn, when focusing is hardest and one idea to try this week, then sees a card of their own picks. That is reflecting on one's own strengths and growth areas and choosing a small goal. Limit: about a minute long; nothing saved or scored.

alignments.framework: New York State Social Emotional Learning Benchmarks (Equity Revisions)
alignments.rationale: Tune Your Brain game "What Helps Me" (tagged self-awareness). FNE's catalog description: "Pick what helps you learn and focus, then try one idea. Only you see it." The last question picks one thing to try this week, which is a small goal. Limit: there is no follow-up on whether it worked.

alignments.framework: New York State Social Emotional Learning Benchmarks (Equity Revisions)
alignments.rationale: Tune Your Brain game "What Helps Me" (tagged self-awareness). FNE's catalog description: "Pick what helps you learn and focus, then try one idea. Only you see it." Knowing how you learn best is part of knowing yourself, and the options include outside supports such as a quiet spot, a friend or a list of steps. Limit: about learning habits, not identity or background.

alignments.framework: New York State Social Emotional Learning Benchmarks (Equity Revisions)
alignments.rationale: Tune Your Brain game "Stuck on It" (tagged self-management). FNE's catalog description: "Read about someone who is stuck, then pick what helps and find the proof." The child reads about someone who is stuck (a hard math problem, learning to ride a bike, a report not yet started), picks what helps (rest, try again with a small goal, write one small part today) and finds the sentence that proves it. That is working toward a goal and recovering from a setback. Limit: reading-based scenes; the child does not set their own goal.

alignments.framework: New York State Social Emotional Learning Benchmarks (Equity Revisions)
alignments.rationale: Tune Your Brain game "Stuck on It" (tagged self-management). FNE's catalog description: "Read about someone who is stuck, then pick what helps and find the proof." Several items start with noticing a feeling such as frustration or worry and calming it before trying again. Limit: the character's feelings, not the player's own.

alignments.framework: New York State Portrait of a Graduate
alignments.rationale: Tune Your Brain game "Stuck on It" (tagged self-management). FNE's catalog description: "Read about someone who is stuck, then pick what helps and find the proof." The best answers set a small goal and keep going after a setback. Limit: about someone else; there is no reflection on the player's own strengths.

alignments.framework: New York State Social Emotional Learning Benchmarks (Equity Revisions)
alignments.rationale: Tune Your Brain game "Team Mission" (tagged relationship skills). FNE's catalog description: "Read a group work problem, pick the best team move, then find the sentence that shows why." The player reads a group work problem (two classmates arguing over who goes first, a quiet teammate with an idea, a partner who will not share the computer), picks the best team move and finds the sentence that shows why. Splitting jobs, inviting a quiet teammate in and asking for turns are communication and social skills used in a group. Limit: group work at grades 3 to 5; not across cultural differences.

alignments.framework: New York State Social Emotional Learning Benchmarks (Equity Revisions)
alignments.rationale: Tune Your Brain game "Team Mission" (tagged relationship skills). FNE's catalog description: "Read a group work problem, pick the best team move, then find the sentence that shows why." Several items start with an argument or a hurt feeling in the group, and the best move settles it. Limit: small group-work conflicts.

alignments.framework: New York State Portrait of a Graduate
alignments.rationale: Tune Your Brain game "Team Mission" (tagged relationship skills). FNE's catalog description: "Read a group work problem, pick the best team move, then find the sentence that shows why." Best moves include asking a quiet teammate what they think and proposing a fair switch, which are speaking and listening skills. Limit: choosing among options; no free writing.

alignments.framework: New York State Social Emotional Learning Benchmarks (Equity Revisions)
alignments.rationale: Tune Your Brain game "Know Your Triggers" (tagged self-awareness and self-management). FNE's catalog description: "Name what raises your stress and how you notice it first. The student picks up to three things that make stress rise, what they notice first (such as a tight chest, racing thoughts or snapping at people), and what could help them notice it sooner. That is identifying one's own emotions and how they show up in what one does. Nothing is saved or scored.

alignments.framework: New York State Portrait of a Graduate
alignments.rationale: Tune Your Brain game "Know Your Triggers" (tagged self-awareness and self-management). FNE's catalog description: "Name what raises your stress and how you notice it first. Limit: it is a short reflection and not a screening; it does not ask about goals or strengths.

Decide what you notice and what to do." In the story a classmate, Sam, has quietly been left out of the project group chat, and the player decides what to do about it. Acting so that a classmate is included is acting for the well-being of the school community. Limit: one story with one classmate.

alignments.framework: New York State Portrait of a Graduate
alignments.rationale: Tune Your Brain game "Decision Point" (tagged social awareness, relationship skills and responsible decision-making). FNE's catalog description: "A classmate is being left out. Decide what you notice and what to do." The situation takes place in a class group chat, and the best moves treat the classmate fairly and bring him back in. alignments.rationale: Tune Your Brain game "Decision Point" (tagged social awareness, relationship skills and responsible decision-making). FNE's catalog description: "A classmate is being left out. Decide what you notice and what to do." The player picks how to approach Sam and the group, which uses communication and social skills with care for the other person. Limit: one step of five.

The player picks ways to handle how they feel before answering and ends with one strategy that helps them pause. That ties a strong emotion to a planned action, which is the skill the benchmark describes.

alignments.framework: New York State Social Emotional Learning Benchmarks (Equity Revisions)
alignments.rationale: Tune Your Brain game "Group Chat Meltdown" (tagged self-management and responsible decision-making). FNE's catalog description: "The chat turned on you. Decide how to answer before you type." The player decides how to respond to the friend who posted it, including telling an adult if it keeps happening. alignments.framework: New York State Portrait of a Graduate
alignments.rationale: Tune Your Brain game "Group Chat Meltdown" (tagged self-management and responsible decision-making). FNE's catalog description: "The chat turned on you. Decide how to answer before you type." The situation is a group chat, and the best moves pause before posting, respond to one friend and report it if it keeps happening. That is acting responsibly in a digital community. Limit: one story about a chat among friends.

alignments.rationale: Tune Your Brain game "Group Chat Meltdown" (tagged self-management and responsible decision-making). FNE's catalog description: "The chat turned on you. FNE's catalog description: "Read a situation, pick the message this person would hear best, then find the sentence that shows why." The player reads a situation (for example cancelling plans with a friend who minds when no new plan is offered), picks the message that person would hear best and finds the sentence that shows what they need. That is communicating with empathy for the particular person in the interaction. Limit: written messages in everyday situations.

alignments.framework: New York State Portrait of a Graduate
alignments.rationale: Tune Your Brain game "Say It Another Way" (tagged relationship skills and social awareness). FNE's catalog description: "Read a situation, pick the message this person would hear best, then find the sentence that shows why." Choosing the clearest, kindest wording for a message and explaining why it works is expressing ideas clearly in writing. Limit: the player chooses among written drafts and does not write their own.

alignments.framework: New York State Social Emotional Learning Benchmarks (Equity Revisions)
alignments.rationale: Tune Your Brain game "Say It Another Way" (tagged relationship skills and social awareness). FNE's catalog description: "Read a situation, pick the message this person would hear best, then find the sentence that shows why." The student reads a situation (a teammate who has stopped answering, a friend keeping borrowed notes, a joke that bothers a teammate), picks the message that is clear and kind and finds what the person needs. That is using communication skills with empathy in the interaction. Limit: choosing among written messages.

alignments.framework: New York State Portrait of a Graduate
alignments.rationale: Tune Your Brain game "Speak Up Kindly" (tagged relationship skills). FNE's catalog description: "Read a situation, pick the message that is clear and kind, then find what is needed." Picking wording that states a need clearly without blame is expressing ideas clearly. Limit: the student chooses among written messages and does not write their own.

alignments.rationale: Tune Your Brain game "Speak Up Kindly" (tagged relationship skills). Seeing how someone else is affected online is the empathy skill the benchmark describes.

alignments.rationale: Tune Your Brain game "Other Side of the Screen" (tagged social awareness). Seeing that people feel and react differently because of their own situations is the skill the benchmark describes.

alignments.rationale: Tune Your Brain game "Peer Pressure Pause" (tagged responsible decision-making). FNE's catalog description: "Read a pressure situation, pick the best choice, then find the risk that proves it." The best choices protect the student's own well-being and relationships.
